— So what do you do?

— I work in acoustics.

— Ah, shengxue. As in childbirth? You’re in obstetrics? Oh, sheng as in sound! So you’re a musician? You sell speakers?

— No, I…

(In Mandarin, shengxue, “acoustics,” sounds as if it could mean “the study of giving birth.”) That ellipsis stands for the inner monologue of every working acoustician.

I have been doing acoustics outreach for over a year now, and with 2020 being the International Year of Sound, it feels like time to pull out the most basic questions and talk about them on their own. Today, two of them:

What is acoustics, and what do acousticians actually do?

What is acoustics?

The word acoustics comes from the Greek ακούειν (akouein), “to hear” [1]. Wikipedia defines it like this:

Acoustics is a branch of physics that deals with the study of mechanical waves in gases, liquids, and solids, including topics such as vibration, sound, ultrasound and infrasound.

To my mind that definition is a bit too stern, and a little one-sided. So let’s work out what acoustics really is in plain language, with the odd joke thrown in.

Acoustics is the science of sound. In other words, anything that has to do with sound falls within its scope. Something produces a sound, the sound travels through one medium or another, and an organ that can hear, such as an ear, picks it up and perceives it. Every link in that chain is acoustics.

Hearing is vital to animal survival, and speech was key to human development and to building culture. So acoustics reaches into every corner of human activity and society: music, medicine, architecture, industry, the environment, even war. And not only among humans: animals, too, rely on sound for the essentials of life, such as courtship and the occasional gang brawl.

Let’s see how many branches of acoustics I touched while writing this very article.

Turn on my computer and put some music on Spotify

— Musicians play their instruments, a singer sings, and recording equipment captures the sound. Spotify plays the file through my speakers. Part of the sound reaches my ears directly; the rest bounces around my room before it gets there. There is sound-absorbing material under the floor, and the sofa and curtains are good absorbers too. All of this shapes what I hear.

— Fields involved: musical instruments, music, recording (microphones, preamplifiers, data acquisition), audio engineering, sound system engineering, room acoustics, sound-absorbing materials.

Type on the keyboard

— The sound of a keyboard is designed as well. An Apple keyboard sounds different from a Lenovo one, and both sound different from a mechanical keyboard.

— Fields involved: mechanical engineering, acoustic design, industrial design.

After a while, walk to the window and open it for some fresh air

— The moment the window opens, I hear the traffic in the street. There are all kinds of cars out there, and each one’s engine note and pass-by sound is a little different.

— Fields involved: environmental noise, building acoustics, automotive acoustics.

Pick up my phone and send a friend a few voice messages

— I speak into the microphone and listen to my friend’s replies on Bose headphones. When I can’t be bothered to listen, I convert the voice message to text.

— Fields involved: microphone technology, DSP, active noise cancellation, audio compression, speech recognition.

Honestly, until I wrote it down I hadn’t noticed how many fields a few minutes of everyday activity could touch. That is what acoustics is like: thoroughly interdisciplinary.

Allow me to introduce the famous Wheel of Acoustics.

Few fundamental sciences are as interdisciplinary as acoustics [https://acoustics.byu.edu/content/what-acoustics]

What do acousticians actually do?

The acoustics website of the University of Salford has a nice diagram:

In one of my earlier outreach talks, I also sketched out the areas acoustics touches:

The Acoustical Society of America (ASA) divides acoustics into the following areas:

Aeroacoustics: how sound and noise are generated by gas flow and how they propagate. Examples include how spacecraft and wind turbines produce noise, and how wind instruments make their sound.

Simulation of the turbulence around a rotating wind turbine

Audio signal processing: a broad field. For example:

  • analog audio signal processing, which involves electrical engineering;

  • sound enhancement, for instance in highly reverberant spaces;

  • noise removal, such as Skype’s echo cancellation or noise reduction in hearing aids;

  • audio compression, such as the famous MP3;

  • audio recognition, such as shaking your phone in WeChat to identify a song.

Architectural acoustics: I have covered the history of architectural acoustics in detail before, so I won’t go into it here.

A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics

Bioacoustics: mainly how animals produce and hear sound. That includes how vocal communication relates to animal behavior and the evolution of species, the mechanisms and neurophysiology of animal hearing, using sound to monitor animal populations, the effect of man-made noise on animals, and more. In my article on AI and acoustics, I also described how artificial intelligence is being applied in bioacoustics.

A history of acoustics: AI in acoustics

Electroacoustics: the reproduction, recording and design of sound in systems such as headphones, microphones and loudspeakers. Electroacoustics has grown rapidly with the rise of phones and other portable electronics, and hi-fi enthusiasts have given it a big push as well. Most electronics companies in the field do some electroacoustic research.

Environmental acoustics: controlling the noise and vibration produced in our surroundings by traffic, aircraft, industrial equipment, entertainment and so on. Practitioners need to measure noise quantitatively and come up with solutions. Many acoustic consultancies offer these services, and plenty of people work in the field, in China and abroad. Because environmental noise is closely tied to health and affects people more and more, it is getting ever more attention. Soundscape, a newer offshoot of environmental acoustics, is the rising star: it looks not only at noise but also at how to use sound positively, in people’s service. For more on soundscapes, see Jian Kang’s book [4].

https://www.nps.gov/yose/learn/nature/soundscape.htm

Musical acoustics: the physics and perception of music. This covers the function and design of musical instruments and electronic synthesizers, the human singing voice, computer analysis and synthesis of music (a former colleague of mine studied computational music in Finland), music therapy in medicine, and more.

How many singers has Auto-Tune rescued from a live trainwreck?

Noise control: as the name suggests, how to reduce noise. You can attack it in three places: at the source, along the transmission path, and at the receiver (with earplugs, say). Noise control includes an important industrial branch, NVH (noise, vibration, and harshness), which plays a huge role in the automotive industry. After N and V, the H is getting more and more attention too, and that brings us to psychoacoustics.

Psychoacoustics: where acoustics meets psychology, and a rising star in the field. The black box that is the human brain brings no end of uncertainty and challenges to acoustics. I have written about it at length before, so I won’t expand on it here.

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 2

Speech: the production, processing and perception of speech, drawing on physics, physiology, psychology, speech signal processing and linguistics. In AI and machine learning, speech recognition and semantic analysis are two major topics. Getting speech transmitted and received clearly, efficiently and with high quality is one of the hard problems in voice interaction today. I touched on this in the AI article mentioned above.

Ultrasonics: ultrasound is too high in frequency for humans to hear, but it is widely used in medicine. Other applications include non-destructive testing and underwater acoustics.

Underwater acoustics: after all that time above the surface, finally something below it. The classic problem in underwater acoustics is locating sound sources underwater, which has wide military use. Beyond human activity, underwater acoustics also overlaps with bioacoustics in the study of marine animals.

http://www.sercel.com/products/Pages/mats3g.aspx

Vibration and dynamics: the vibration of mechanical systems. Examples include ground vibration from railway tracks, vibration isolation of buildings (anechoic chambers, for instance), human vibration (hand-arm vibration syndrome), protecting bridges against earthquakes, structure-borne sound in buildings, and so on.

Beyond the ASA’s categories, I would add a few more of my own (some overlap with the ones above):

medical acoustics, materials acoustics and virtual acoustics.

On virtual acoustics, I have written a history of auralization:

A history of acoustics: auralization

Finally, hear it from acousticians themselves:

https://exploresound.org/meet-acousticians/

Fellow acousticians, additions, comments and suggestions are very welcome.

And I hope the epidemic recedes soon and life gets back to normal. Stay safe and healthy, everyone!

If you’re stuck at home with time on your hands, a bit of acoustics reading isn’t a bad way to spend it ^^
